title: Indian Rappers Turn Water Shortages and Heat Into a Climate Alarm
excerpt: Kali, Abisha of Sollisai Sistahs and four other young artistes have released the six-track Climate Emergency Mixtape, billed as India's first multilingual rap album about the climate crisis.
body:
• Six tracks make up the "Climate Emergency Mixtape," billed by its organisers as India's first multilingual rap album about the climate crisis, according to AFP.
  • Bengaluru rapper Kali's "Neer Kodu" ("Give Water" in Kannada) draws on his childhood memories of hauling plastic pots from a public tap about 10 minutes from home.
  • Tamil rapper Abisha of Sollisai Sistahs, Tamil Nadu's first all-women rap crew, wrote "Veppa Marathadiyila" ("Under the Neem Tree") about climate change's impact on marginalised communities.
  • Collaborator Brikesh Singh of Asar Social Impact Advisors says music is an extremely powerful medium for reaching people who are living the climate crisis.

Indian rapper Kali needed little inspiration to write about dwindling water supplies. He drew on childhood memories of hauling plastic pots full of the precious resource, AFP reported in a story carried by The Peninsula Times and Singapore's Tabla. His track "Neer Kodu" — "Give Water" in Kannada — is one of six tracks on the "Climate Emergency Mixtape," billed by its organisers as India's first multilingual rap album about the climate crisis.

Kali, 29, whose real name is Akshay, grew up in Bengaluru and has been making music for more than a decade, citing Eminem and Akon as influences. As a child, he walked for around 10 minutes to fill pots with water from a public tap. "We would always think... we should not waste this," he told AFP during the album launch this month.

Water as Lived Experience

Water shortages are a chronic problem in Bengaluru, India's tech hub, where many residents rely on groundwater wells that often run dry in summer. Others depend on expensive water trucked in from elsewhere. Climate change threatens to worsen that stress as temperatures rise and weather patterns shift.

In a separate interview with Indulge Express at the album's Bengaluru launch, Kali explained how uneven the city is: in south and central Bengaluru, trees and parks are still preserved, while in his neighbourhood daily life revolves around when the power cut will happen and how much water must last the week. Access, he said, is rooted in class and caste. He also argued that the burden should not fall on working-class and marginalised people alone: "we might all follow sustainable practices, but one move by a billionaire and all our efforts are gone."

Six Tracks, Six Landscapes

The mixtape brings together six independent young artistes, each writing from a specific place. Naveen Koomar's "Vann Katte" is about the Aravalli ridge near his childhood home in Firozpur Jhirka, a range he has watched shrink under mining, real estate lobbies and rapid urbanisation. Devanshi!'s "Nisargacha Kaayda" warns that chasing profit alone ends in loss, and speaks for animals, indigenous tribes and farmers. Alkama's "Nasht Environment" channels growing up amid chronic pollution, and Gamak Sinha's "Soil" gives the ground itself a voice, from discovery to destruction.

The fifth track, "Veppa Marathadiyila" — "Under the Neem Tree" in Tamil — comes from Abisha of Sollisai Sistahs. The 26-year-old remembers water reaching her doorstep when she was around eight; two years later, she told AFP, the area had run dry. She said climate change is still not spoken about widely in her community, and hopes the song will reach people more powerfully than spoken words alone.

"If we want to reach out to people who are experiencing the climate crisis, we need to change how society tells those stories. Music, we felt, is an extremely powerful medium."

— Brikesh Singh, Asar Social Impact Advisors

Why Rap, Why Now

India, the world's most populous country and its third-largest greenhouse gas emitter, is vulnerable to extreme weather. While some areas have faced drought, others have suffered deadly floods and landslides triggered by heavy rain. The album's collaborators, including Asar Social Impact Advisors, argue that the people experiencing that crisis first are often the last to be heard in how the story is told.

Kali urged more artists to move beyond subjects such as cars and bikes, which he called "boring." "They should talk about something that actually matters — which is climate change," he said.

For diaspora listeners, the mixtape offers something statistics rarely do: the climate crisis in the languages and neighbourhoods of home — Kannada, Tamil and more — told by artists who queued at public taps, watched lakes and ridges disappear, and decided the most direct route to a listener was a beat.
